idiom_name: ES module top-level evaluation (once per module instance) / require cache
implementation_notes: A module is evaluated at most once per module instance, so top-level initialization is the idiom: ES modules run their body on first import (MDN's modules guide describes modules as evaluated once within their own scope) and Node's CommonJS loader caches modules by resolved filename, so later require calls return the same exports object instead of re-executing the module (the Node docs state this explicitly). Deferred construction is a closure with a memoized accessor (`??=`) or a module-scoped variable; no guard object and no counter are needed, because the module registry supplies the once-only guarantee.
pitfalls: The guarantee is per module instance, not per process: a package loaded once as ESM and once as CommonJS (the dual-package hazard), a bundler that duplicates the module, worker threads, or a fresh server-side module registry each create another 'singleton'.
Circular imports expose partially evaluated modules: an imported binding can be in its temporal dead zone (or undefined under CommonJS) if the module body reads it during the cycle.

require.cache is mutable and keyed by resolved filename: deleting an entry re-executes the module (useful in tests, a trap elsewhere), and different specifiers or symlinked paths can duplicate the instance.
Module top-level side effects run at import time even when nothing consumes the export, unless the value is deliberately made lazy.
